name: stone
desc: TCP/IP packet repeater in the application layer
why: An application-layer TCP/IP packet repeater, an obscure and unusual door into how packets can be relayed at the application layer.

brief.what_it_is: Stone is a small TCP/IP repeater that runs at the application layer, relaying TCP and UDP traffic from inside a firewall to outside, or from outside to inside. You run it with a listen spec and a destination spec (for example, stone outer:telnet 10023), and it forwards the connection between them. The page also describes it as a tiny http proxy, an SSL wrapper that can encrypt a plain service, a POP-to-APOP bridge, and an IPv4/IPv6 converter.
brief.why_it_exists: The author frames it for firewalls: UNIX machines used to be the usual firewalls, but Windows NT machines are now used too, so Stone was written to run on Windows as well as Unix-like systems. He also stresses that it is simple, at about 10000 lines of C, so the risk of security holes is minimized.
brief.how_it_works: Stone listens on a local or named port and opens a connection to the target you name, then copies data between the two sides. Optional wrappers are added per endpoint with suffixes such as /udp, /ssl, /http, /proxy, and /apop, which change how that side speaks. SSL uses OpenSSL and can verify client and server certificates, and it can pass a substring of the certificate subject to the destination.

commands_seen.context: Repeats telnet to the machine named outer; on the inner machine you then run telnet fwall 10023.
Repeats DNS queries over UDP to outer; the inner side uses nslookup - fwall.
Repeats NTP over UDP to outer; the inner side runs ntpdate fwall.
Makes a WWW server that speaks https on port 443 by wrapping the local http port in SSL; reach it at https://fwall/.
Makes a telnet server that supports SSL; the inner client connects with SSLtelnet -z ssl fwall 10023.
Runs Stone as a tiny http proxy listening on port 8080.
Lets a mailer that lacks APOP reach an APOP POP server: it connects to inner:pop through the converter.
Tunnels a stream through an http proxy on fwall port 8080, using the quoted POST line as the request; paired with a second stone run on outer.
The outer-side half of the http tunnel example; run on the outside machine to accept the relayed stream.
Local listener on 9080 that adds a Proxy-Authorization header, for a browser that cannot send proxy credentials itself.

brief.install_notes: Pre-built Windows binaries are listed for version 2.3e (Win64, Win32, WinXP, WinNT/2000, Win98), and there is an official 2.4 release and a 2.4 source snapshot. Source is C, built from stone.c; the page mentions a CVS repository on SourceForge.JP. SSL needs OpenSSL. POP-to-APOP conversion needs an MD5 program installed. Mailing list sign-up is by email to stone-subscribe@gcd.org. The page does not give explicit build steps.
brief.standout: It is an old, self-described 'Simple Repeater' that bundles a TCP/UDP relay, SSL termination, http tunneling, a proxy, POP-to-APOP conversion, and IPv4/IPv6 translation into one small C program. The http tunnel example, which carries a stream inside HTTP POST through an ordinary proxy, is a neat trick for getting past restrictive firewalls.
brief.status: quiet. The latest official release, version 2.4, is dated 02/15/19. The page says it was last modified 08/14/21 and carries a 1995-2021 copyright. The author mentions a development diary and a CVS repository, but I saw no recent release or commit date.
brief.caveats: The page is dated and the Windows binaries are for 2.3e, not 2.4. It is a firewall-era tool, so think carefully before exposing it. The text is in English but the articles and diary are in Japanese. The page does not state a license. Build and SSL setup details are thin, and the examples assume you can reach both sides of a firewall. Homebrew's caveats field is empty.
quotes: Stone is a TCP/IP repeater in the application layer.
Stone's source code is only 10000 lines long (written in C language), so you can minimize the risk of security holes.
Stone can also be a tiny http proxy.
